channel.title: Joseph Bankole's news desk
channel.description: A running digest of payments, agentic commerce, and the AI stories that touch how money moves. Sourced, edited, and written plainly, by Joseph Bankole.

item.title: Amazon blocks Meta's Muse agent from Amazon.com
item.description: Amazon blocked Meta's Muse agent from buying on Amazon.com on 20 September 2026. Shopify said the next morning that Shop Pay will check out with Muse.
item.content:encoded:
Amazon has stopped letting Meta’s Muse agent buy anything on Amazon.com. GeekWire’s Todd Bishop published the story at 11:05 pm on Sunday 20 September 2026 and updated it at 10:49 am the next morning, writing that “as of Sunday night, people trying to use Muse to shop on Amazon were seeing the popup” [1]. implicator.ai dates the block to 20 September as well [2].

Amazon’s statement to GeekWire does not mention payments once. “We think it’s fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate”, it reads, and “Agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations, and we’ve requested that Meta remove Amazon from the experience” [1]. Asked whether it would take legal action, Amazon declined to comment, and Meta did not immediately respond to GeekWire’s request that Sunday night [1]. Meta’s own line on Muse is about credential handling: the agent “has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods”, and credentials “go into secure storage, so Muse can use them without seeing them, including passwords a person types into the browser themselves” [1].

The two statements answer different questions. Meta is describing how the agent holds a card, while Amazon is describing who decides whether the agent is let in at all. Checkout was always the solved half of Muse: the 21 September edition of this brief traced it to Stripe’s Link wallet issuing a single-use virtual card scoped to the approved purchase, good at more than a million businesses that accept Link [3]. A single-use card number has nothing to say to a retailer who declines to be in the basket at all.

What the scale numbers do and do not say

GeekWire puts Amazon’s advertising revenue last year at $68 billion, and notes that Muse was the number one free app on Apple’s United States App Store a week after its 8 September 2026 launch [1]. Axios, carrying the story the same day, reaches for two forecasts: Coveo’s 2026 Commerce Relevance Report puts at 16 per cent the share of shoppers comfortable letting an AI assistant find and buy products for them, and McKinsey’s estimate is up to $1 trillion of United States retail revenue from AI-mediated search and purchase automation by 2030 [4]. The 16 per cent measures stated comfort in a survey and the trillion is a projection four years out. Neither is a count of agent purchases, and nobody has published one of those.

Shopify went the other way inside a day

On the morning of 21 September 2026 Shopify’s chief executive, Tobi Lütke, said the company is “partnering deeply with Muse to enable agentic checkout with Shop Pay on all Shopify stores”. That is quoted from his own post by implicator.ai; the post returns HTTP 402 to a reader without an account, so the carrier is the only version of it available here [2]. American Banker’s John Adams had the Shopify strategy on 18 September and updated the piece on 21 September [5]. The business it bolts onto is substantial. Shopify reported second-quarter gross merchandise volume of $116 billion, up 32 per cent, with Shopify Payments taking 68 per cent of that volume, 75 per cent of Shop Pay customers using it again within twelve months, and Shop Pay’s average order value running about 16 per cent above a non-Shop Pay order [5]. Shopify’s vice-president of product, Rohit Mishra, told American Banker that “agentic commerce really excites us. The agents don’t have the same challenges as humans” [5].

One agent now carries two merchant-side wallets: Link across the Link network, Shop Pay across Shopify’s. The routing question stops being which rail wins and becomes a per-merchant lookup your code has to make before it offers a button. A partnership is not a shipped feature, and neither Lütke nor American Banker gives a date on which a shopper can actually use it [2] [5].

The first calendar entry

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission announced a roundtable series on 21 September 2026, press release 9301-26, and the opening Frontier Forum falls on 28 October 2026 with artificial intelligence and agentic finance as its subject [6]. Chairman Michael S. Selig’s line is that “the technologies transforming our markets are rapidly advancing, and the CFTC must engage directly with the people building, using, and studying them”, and speaker nominations go in by email [6]. PYMNTS carried it the same day [7]. There is no proposed rule in the release and no comment deadline, and payments and checkout are not mentioned anywhere in it. The commission’s remit is derivatives, so agentic finance here does not mean agentic commerce [6].

Nothing else in agentic commerce or payments carried a number worth printing between 20 and 22 September 2026. The Know Your Agent interoperability framework, the Alchemy and Mastercard Agent Pay tie-up and the CFTC’s passive-software-provider guidance all landed earlier in the month and are already in this desk’s archive.

Amazon asked Meta to take Amazon out of Muse on the same weekend Shopify offered Muse every store it has.

Sources

  1. GeekWire, Todd Bishop, “Amazon blocks Meta’s Muse AI assistant in new standoff over agentic shopping”, 21 September 2026, read 22 September 2026
  2. implicator.ai, Marcus Schuler, “Amazon and Shopify split over Meta’s Muse agent”, 21 September 2026, read 22 September 2026
  3. Stripe newsroom, “Stripe helps Muse, Meta’s new personal AI agent, shop across the internet with Link”, 8 September 2026, read 21 September 2026
  4. Axios, Nathan Bomey, “Amazon kicks Meta’s Muse off its site”, 21 September 2026, read 22 September 2026 via the Yahoo Finance syndication
  5. American Banker, John Adams, “Shopify adds Meta’s Muse to its agentic AI strategy”, 18 September 2026, updated 21 September 2026, read 22 September 2026
  6. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, press release 9301-26, “CFTC Innovation Task Force to Host Frontier Forum Series on Innovative Financial Technologies”, 21 September 2026, read 22 September 2026
  7. PYMNTS, “CFTC Examines Agentic AI’s Growing Role in Finance”, 21 September 2026, read 22 September 2026

item.title: Stripe's Link now checks out for three AI agents
item.description: Stripe's Link wallet checks out for Meta's Muse, xAI's Grok Bot and Instinct. Each agent buys with a single-use virtual card scoped to that purchase.
item.content:encoded:
Stripe’s Link wallet now checks out for at least three separate AI agents, and each of them buys the same way. The consumer approves the total inside the chat, and the agent is handed a card number that works once [1].

Meta put Link inside Muse, its personal agent, on 8 September 2026 [2] [7]. Stripe’s own note on that release says Muse can check out instantly at “more than 1 million businesses that accept Link” using a US consumer’s saved payment method, that “for every purchase, consumers are asked to approve the transaction total directly in the chat interface, and Muse never sees their underlying payment details”, and that everywhere else “Link issues Muse a single-use virtual card scoped to the approved purchase” [2]. Stripe puts Link at 300 million users [2], a figure Payments Dive carried on 18 September 2026 next to the roughly one million merchants [1].

Muse was not the first. Payments Dive reports that Stripe introduced Link payments for AI agents at its annual developer conference in April 2026, and that xAI’s Grok Bot and Instinct, a text-message assistant built by Spear Street Technology, were both wired to Link before Meta was [1]. Crypto Briefing dates the Grok Bot launch to 28 August 2026 and says every transaction still needs an explicit human approval before money moves [3]. The same outlet puts the feature behind xAI’s $200-a-month tier, which no other outlet carries, so that figure has one source. Instinct is invite-only and connects to a user’s email, calendar, screen, audio and location, TechCrunch reported on 24 August 2026 [4].

What the merchant actually sees

Stripe assembled this out of parts that already existed: a consumer wallet, a card network and a virtual card number, arranged so the agent never holds anything it can use twice. Alchemy shipped the same shape on 17 September 2026, one-time, tokenised Mastercard credentials issued against a user’s existing card through Mastercard Agent Pay [8] [9].

An agent purchase routed this way lands as an ordinary card authorisation on a single-use number. Nothing in that message says a machine filled the basket. A merchant who cannot already tell agent traffic from human traffic at the front door will not learn it from the acquiring side, and the question of how much of the quarter an agent brought in waits until somebody reconciles it by hand.

What Stripe tried to buy

Stripe and Advent International offered more than $53 billion for PayPal on 15 July 2026, at $60.50 a share, and PayPal’s board turned it down [5] [6]. Payments Dive’s reading on 18 September 2026 is that Stripe needs PayPal’s consumer network and its spread of funding account types to compete in agentic commerce [1]. Link already has 300 million users, and Stripe bid for PayPal anyway.

Nothing else in agentic commerce or payments moved between 19 and 21 September 2026 that carried a number worth printing. It was a weekend.

For most of 2026 the agentic payments argument has been about which new rail wins, scored on protocol volume. The three agents checking out on a saved card in September 2026 are not on a new rail. They are on a card issued for one purchase, inside a wallet that was already there.

Sources

  1. Payments Dive, Justin Bachman, “Stripe’s wallet embraces AI bots”, 18 September 2026, read 21 September 2026
  2. Stripe newsroom, “Stripe helps Muse, Meta’s new personal AI agent, shop across the internet with Link”, 8 September 2026, read 21 September 2026
  3. Crypto Briefing, “Grok Bot enables online purchases with Stripe Link integration in the US”, 28 August 2026, read 21 September 2026
  4. TechCrunch, “Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns”, 24 August 2026, read 21 September 2026
  5. CNBC, “Stripe, Advent offer to buy PayPal for more than $53 billion”, 15 July 2026, read 21 September 2026
  6. Quartz, “Stripe and Advent International make $53 billion offer for PayPal”, 15 July 2026, read 21 September 2026
  7. The Paypers, “Meta launches Muse AI agent with Stripe Link checkout”, 9 September 2026, read 21 September 2026
  8. Alchemy via PR Newswire, “Alchemy Unlocks AI Agent Purchases Anywhere Mastercard is Accepted Online via AgentCard”, 17 September 2026, read 21 September 2026
  9. PYMNTS, “Mastercard and Alchemy Partner to Enable Everyday Agentic Payments”, 17 September 2026, read 21 September 2026

item.title: HM Treasury drafts carve-out for UK stablecoin payments
item.description: HM Treasury laid a draft instrument on 15 September 2026 taking UK qualifying stablecoins out of the cryptoasset dealing and arranging rules.
item.content:encoded:
HM Treasury laid a draft statutory instrument on 15 September 2026 that pulls UK qualifying stablecoins out of three regulated activities at once: dealing in qualifying cryptoassets as principal, dealing as agent, and arranging deals in qualifying cryptoassets [1] [2] [3]. It is called the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Cryptoassets) (Miscellaneous Amendments) Regulations 2026, and the framework it amends is the Cryptoassets Regulations 2026, S.I. 2026/102 [2].

The explanatory memorandum gives the reason. Without the change, payment activities involving a UK qualifying stablecoin would likely sit inside the cryptoasset dealing and intermediary activities, with stablecoin payment firms carrying “overlapping or disproportionate regulatory requirements ahead of the wider payments reforms coming into force” [2]. HM Treasury consulted in July 2026 on bringing certain stablecoins into the payments perimeter instead [2], so the exclusion holds until the payments regime catches up.

Lending and borrowing stay in. The Government keeps those activities inside the perimeter because of the risk it says they present to consumers and other users, and carves out one exception: institutional collateral and repurchase agreement arrangements come out of the dealing and arranging activities for all qualifying stablecoins, UK-issued or overseas, where the original holder is not a consumer or a person specified by Financial Conduct Authority rules [2]. Norton Rose Fulbright read it the same way on 16 September 2026: transferring a UK qualifying stablecoin or exchanging it for another asset falls outside, except for lending and borrowing arrangements and exchanges for cryptoassets that are not UK qualifying stablecoins [3].

Holding a UK qualifying stablecoin temporarily in connection with a payment transaction also comes out of the cryptoasset safeguarding activity, and backing asset arrangements for those stablecoins come out of the relevant safeguarding activities [2]. The instrument then writes a new controlled activity into the Financial Promotion Order, issuing qualifying stablecoin, and a new controlled investment to go with it [2]. The draft is not law yet. It needs parliamentary approval, and the memorandum dates the cryptoassets regime coming fully into force to 25 October 2027 [2]. Anyone treating it as relief today is planning against a document that has not been made.

Fifteen per cent of merchants have product data an agent can read

PYMNTS Intelligence published “Will the 2026 Shopping Season Go Agentic?” in September 2026, drawing on consumer, merchant and acquirer research run between September 2025 and August 2026, with a latest wave of 2,061 US consumers and 60 US retail merchants [6]. Sixty merchants is a small room, and every merchant figure in that report rests on it. PYMNTS puts nearly 132 million US adults as having bought a retail product with AI’s help, and 59% of AI-assisted purchases as still ending at Amazon [5], figures Forkast News carried on 15 September 2026 [7].

The readiness figure comes off a larger sample. In PYMNTS’s Global Digital Shopping Index: The Agentic Commerce Deep Dive, published on 8 September 2026 across 1,185 merchants, 5,241 consumers and 150 acquirers in the United States, Brazil and the United Arab Emirates, “just 15% have structured product data an agent can read” [8]. The Merchant Edition of the same index, commissioned by Visa Acceptance Solutions, reported on 2 September 2026 that 23% of merchants can clearly identify both AI-driven traffic and the purchases that follow, and that 21% can see the traffic and cannot join it to a completed purchase [9]. By size it is 27% of large merchants against 19% of small and medium businesses [9]. A product feed an agent cannot parse throws no error and pages nobody. The merchant finds out at the end of the quarter, if at all.

One investment, and no number attached to it

Azoma, which sells what it calls agentic commerce optimisation, said on 18 September 2026 that it had taken investment from dunnhumby ventures, and that Leo Nagdas, head of dunnhumby ventures, had joined as a board advisor [4]. Max Sinclair, the company’s chief executive and co-founder, is quoted in the release [4]. The release carries no amount, and no independent outlet has reported one, so the size of the round is unknown rather than small.

Nothing else in agentic commerce moved between 18 and 20 September 2026 that carried a number worth printing.

Sources

  1. HM Treasury via GOV.UK, “Draft statutory instrument amending the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Cryptoassets) Regulations 2026: Policy Note”, updated 15 September 2026, read 20 September 2026
  2. HM Treasury, “Explanatory Memorandum to the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Cryptoassets) (Miscellaneous Amendments) Regulations 2026”, legislation.gov.uk, read 20 September 2026
  3. Norton Rose Fulbright, Global Regulation Tomorrow, “Draft SI: The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Cryptoassets) (Miscellaneous Amendments) Regulations 2026”, 16 September 2026, read 20 September 2026
  4. Azoma via GlobeNewswire, “Azoma Receives Investment from dunnhumby ventures to Accelerate its Agentic Commerce Optimization Platform”, London, 18 September 2026, read 20 September 2026
  5. PYMNTS Intelligence, “Will the 2026 Shopping Season Go Agentic?”, September 2026, read 20 September 2026
  6. PYMNTS, “Agentic Shopping: AI Finds, Amazon Sells”, 15 September 2026, read 20 September 2026
  7. Forkast News via Yahoo Finance, Tessa Vaughn, “132 Million Americans Now Shop With AI — and 59% of Those Purchases Still Land on Amazon”, 15 September 2026, read 20 September 2026
  8. PYMNTS, “Merchants Put AI to Work Without Handing Over the Customer”, 8 September 2026, read 20 September 2026
  9. PYMNTS, “How 23% of Merchants Captured Retail’s Next Agentic Commerce Advantage”, 2 September 2026, read 20 September 2026

item.title: OCC gives three stablecoin firms conditional trust charters
item.description: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency gave conditional national trust bank charters to Bastion Platforms, Catena and Agora on 18 September 2026.
item.content:encoded:
On 18 September 2026 the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency gave conditional national trust bank charters to three stablecoin firms, Bastion Platforms, Catena and Agora [1] [2]. Law360 reported that all three plan to expand their stablecoin and crypto offerings as national trust banks [1].

Bastion put out its release that afternoon. As Bastion Platforms National Trust Company it will offer stablecoin custody and wallets, payment infrastructure and white-label issuance “from a single federally regulated entity”, and it says Sony Bank’s global stablecoin initiative runs on Bastion [3]. The charter converts the New York limited-purpose trust charter Bastion took on in February 2025, when it bought Dibbs Trust Company [2] [5]. Crypto Briefing reports that Bastion will take no deposits and carry no FDIC insurance [2], so a treasury policy that lists balances held there alongside insured bank deposits has them in the wrong column.

Catena is the one built around agents. Catena Labs, whose co-founder Sean Neville also co-founded Circle, applied on 18 May 2026 to offer custody, trust, conversion, clearing and execution services across fiat, securities and digital assets, including stablecoins compliant with the GENIUS Act, according to American Banker’s charter tracker [5]. Its tools let a person set spending limits, approved recipients, holding caps and audit trails before an agent handles the money, and The Block reported in May that the charter would make it “a regulated fiduciary for AI agents” [4]. The same tracker records Agora’s application, filed on 24 April, as mainly digital asset custody, investment advisory and stablecoin issuance out of New York [5].

The agent payment rail is carrying less money

Daily payment volume on x402, an open-source rail designed for AI agents, fell from $800,000 in January to about $40,000 in September, a 93% drop, American Banker reported on 18 September 2026 [6]. The same article counts 950 agentic-payment start-ups in Verda Ventures’ index, the largest category among the 6,000 stablecoin-related start-ups it follows, and cites Tracxn’s count of 1,091 agentic AI companies in the first quarter of 2026 [6]. Alex Witt, a general partner at Verda Ventures, told the paper: “The incremental lift to add agentic payments is low, and it will be a leap of faith for businesses to adopt this new tech from startups” [6].

TRM Labs had already looked at what that volume was made of. It examined about 198.9 million x402 transactions worth $52.7 million on Base, Solana and Polygon from May 2025 onwards, and after stripping out non-commercial activity found that only 0.6% to 7.5% of the remaining value looked agentic, PYMNTS reported on 15 September 2026 [7]. A conventional script can run exactly the same payment sequence as an agent, PYMNTS noted, and late-2025 traffic included activity consistent with meme-token minting [7]. For a merchant weighing an x402 integration this quarter, those numbers size a pilot.

Ant International will cover an agent’s mistakes

Ant International launched close to 100 AI products across Alipay+, Antom, WorldFirst and Bettr on 18 September 2026 [8] [9]. Account for Agent is a business account built for autonomous AI agents [9], which Ant describes as running on smart contracts with know-your-agent checks, monitoring and the means to intervene [8]. AgentSafePay offers what the release calls a “100% fund guarantee against losses arising from intent misinterpretation, malicious prompt injection or other agent-specific risks” [8], and FinTech Global described it as a fund-back guarantee against risks such as prompt injection [9]. Neither the release nor FinTech Global gives a cap, a claims window or the test for deciding that an agent caused the loss [8] [9].

Bastion will offer white-label issuance under its conditional federal charter [3], and Treasury is still defining what it means to issue a payment stablecoin in the United States. Its proposed rule on issuing, offering and selling payment stablecoins takes comments until 19 October 2026 [10] [11].

Sources

  1. Law360, Aislinn Keely, “OCC Approves 3 Trust Charters For Stablecoin Businesses”, 18 September 2026, read 19 September 2026
  2. Crypto Briefing, “US OCC grants conditional banking license approval to Bastion”, 18 September 2026, read 19 September 2026
  3. Bastion via GlobeNewswire, “Bastion Receives Conditional OCC Approval for a National Trust Bank Charter”, New York, 18 September 2026, read 19 September 2026
  4. The Block, Naga Avan-Nomayo, “Catena Labs lands $30 million Series A, files for national trust bank charter to underpin agentic finance”, 20 May 2026, read 19 September 2026
  5. American Banker, Melinda Lucy, “Fintechs asking for, and receiving, bank charters in 2026”, 28 April 2026, updated 18 September 2026, read 19 September 2026
  6. American Banker, John Adams, “Is there an agentic payments bubble?”, 18 September 2026, read 19 September 2026
  7. PYMNTS, “Agentic Payments Are Growing, but Most x402 Payments Aren’t From AI Agents”, 15 September 2026, read 19 September 2026
  8. Ant International via PR Newswire APAC, “Ant International Launches Industry’s First Full-Stack AI-Native Solutions for Payment, Account, FX, Treasury and Growth Operations for Global Businesses”, Shanghai and Singapore, 18 September 2026, read 19 September 2026
  9. FinTech Global, “Ant International hands payment control to AI agents”, 18 September 2026, read 19 September 2026

item.title: Circle launches Arc mainnet with Visa and Mastercard
item.description: Circle launched the public mainnet of Arc, a Layer 1 blockchain with fees in USDC, on 16 September 2026. Visa and Mastercard are among its validators.
item.content:encoded:
Circle switched on the public mainnet of Arc on 16 September 2026. It is a Layer 1 blockchain whose fees are paid in USDC, the stablecoin Circle issues, of which more than $74 billion is in circulation [1] [2]. BlackRock, DTCC, ICE, Mastercard, Visa, Standard Chartered and SBI Group are among the founding validators, the validator set is permissioned, and more than 100 institutional and ecosystem builders were live on day one [1] [2].

Circle is selling the chain to agents as hard as to treasurers. Arc Portal lets a person fund an agent wallet, set spend limits and hand it tasks onchain, the release says [1], and Decrypt lists agent wallets, spending limits and nanopayments among what shipped [2]. Circle also says USDC carries 98.8% of agent-driven transaction volume, a figure Decrypt reports it took from Dune [1] [2]. Jeremy Allaire, Circle’s chief executive, said in the release: “The agentic economy and the onchain economy are not two different revolutions; they are the same economy seen from two sides” [1].

Alchemy’s AgentCard now carries Mastercard credentials

A day later Mastercard lent its card rails to a product that also hands agents a stablecoin wallet. Alchemy said on 17 September 2026 that AgentCard, its payments and identity kit for AI agents, now supports Mastercard credentials through Mastercard Agent Pay [3] [4]. An agent set up on it gets a dedicated email address, a phone number, a stablecoin wallet and one-time-use Mastercard credentials. The credentials are tokenised and linked to the user’s existing Mastercard, so its rewards and credit line carry over [3]. Users and issuers set the agent’s purchase limits and allowed merchant categories, and AgentCard is built to support Verifiable Intent, Mastercard’s record of what the user approved [3] [4].

The release splits the job in two. The stablecoin wallet is for the new agent payment protocols, and the card credential is for “the many online merchants that still rely on traditional credit card rails” [3]. Alchemy’s own post on X was shorter: “The checkout button is dying” [4]. PYMNTS noted that Alchemy wired AgentCard into Visa Intelligent Commerce in June [4].

Cloudflare blocks the agent at the ad

Since 15 September 2026, Cloudflare has offered new domains that earn money from ads a preset that allows search crawlers, refuses AI training and blocks agents on any page detected serving an ad [5] [6]. The agent category covers user-directed agents visiting for a person, such as chat fetch bots and browser-use agents [5] [6]. Bryan Becker wrote in Cloudflare’s announcement that “Ad revenue depends on a human actually seeing the page”, and that agents “fetch the page with nobody there to see the ads” [5].

Fewer than 1% of Cloudflare sites block search bots and 17% block training, the company said [5] [6]. There is no Disallow setting for agents yet, only a block [5] [6]. PYMNTS pointed out that the block lands hardest on the review sites and comparison guides a shopping agent reads before it reaches a checkout [6].

Alchemy says an agent on AgentCard can now pay anywhere Mastercard is accepted online [3]. Will the review site it reads first let it in, or send it a bill for the visit?

Sources

  1. Circle, “Circle Launches Arc Mainnet, an Economic Operating System for the Internet”, New York, 16 September 2026, read 18 September 2026
  2. Decrypt, “Circle Launches Arc Mainnet With BlackRock, DTCC and Visa as Validators”, 16 September 2026, read 18 September 2026
  3. Alchemy via PR Newswire, “Alchemy Unlocks AI Agent Purchases Anywhere Mastercard is Accepted Online via AgentCard”, San Francisco, 17 September 2026, read 18 September 2026
  4. PYMNTS, “Mastercard and Alchemy Partner on Everyday Agentic Payments”, 17 September 2026, read 18 September 2026
  5. Cloudflare Blog, Bryan Becker, “Have it both ways: stay discoverable in search while disallowing AI training”, 15 September 2026, read 18 September 2026
  6. PYMNTS, “Cloudflare Blocks AI Agents From Ad-Supported Pages”, 17 September 2026, read 18 September 2026

item.title: Google adds cart transfer to merchant sites for UCP checkout
item.description: Google said on 16 September 2026 that merchants using Universal Commerce Protocol checkout can transfer the cart to their own site, starting in the US.
item.content:encoded:
Google’s checkout, which sells in Search, AI Mode and the Gemini app, can now hand the cart back to the merchant. On 16 September 2026 Ashish Gupta, Google’s VP and general manager of merchant shopping, wrote that merchants using the Universal Commerce Protocol integration hub in Merchant Center for UCP-powered checkout can turn on cart transfer to their own site and enhanced checkout flow testing, with analytics “and more coming soon” [1]. The features are rolling out gradually in the US, with Australia and Canada to follow early in 2027 [1] [2].

Google says UCP already runs direct checkout for hundreds of thousands of brands and retailers, and it named Tapestry, owner of Coach and Kate Spade, as one that integrated in time for the gifting season [1]. With cart transfer switched on, Google sends the shopper’s cart to the merchant’s own site.

The same post made AI performance insights generally available in Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand and the US. It compares a retailer’s share of voice with other brands in AI Mode and AI Overviews [1]. Google also opened a US beta that puts its Business Agent inside YouTube ads, and said that in testing with lululemon, the brand’s conversational attributes were used 50% of the time in relevant product recommendations in AI Mode [1].

Mastercard built Trip.com’s agent on its merchant suite

Mastercard and Trip.com showed TripGenie, Trip.com’s AI agent, searching, booking and paying for travel on Mastercard’s Agent Suite for Merchants, with Network International as acquirer, TradeArabia reported from Dubai on 16 September 2026 [3] [4]. It is a showcase at Arabian Travel Market. The partners expect a phased rollout and a commercial launch in early 2027, starting with selected services such as attractions and ancillary offerings [3].

Mete Güney, Mastercard’s executive vice president for market development in EEMEA, said the suite lets merchants “remain in control of their brand and customer engagements” [3]. Schubert Lou, Trip.com’s chief executive, described agents “operating securely and with the traveler’s authorization” [3]. Mastercard sells the suite through Mastercard Merchant Cloud, next to its fraud protection, authentication and tokenisation services [3].

PYMNTS, covering Google’s release the same day, quoted its own research predicting that “Merchants will try to steer shoppers to their own agents inside their own closed ecosystems” [2]. In the same research, 24% of consumers surveyed would let an AI agent shop and buy for them, and 14% would let an AI app hold their card [2].

Sources

  1. Google, Ashish Gupta, “Boost your holiday sales with these agentic commerce updates”, 16 September 2026, read 17 September 2026
  2. PYMNTS on Google’s agentic commerce updates and PYMNTS Intelligence consumer research, 16 September 2026, read 17 September 2026
  3. Mastercard’s own release on Trip.com, TripGenie and Agent Suite for Merchants, Mastercard EEMEA newsroom, September 2026, read 17 September 2026
  4. TradeArabia, “Mastercard, Trip.com partner to transform travel booking with AI”, Dubai, 16 September 2026, read 17 September 2026

item.title: India's NPCI holds back its AI agent protocol for UPI
item.description: NPCI held back the Unified Agent Protocol for Reserve Bank of India clearance. Amazon Pay, Razorpay, Pine Labs and BharatPe shipped agent payments anyway.
item.content:encoded:
The Unified Agent Protocol was to be India’s national standard for letting an AI agent pay on UPI without a person approving each transaction, and it was expected at Global Fintech Fest in Mumbai during the week of 8 September 2026 [2]. It did not arrive. NPCI told the industry late on the Wednesday night that it was holding the protocol back pending Reserve Bank of India clearance, India Fintech Diaries reported on 15 September 2026 [1].

NPCI had already drawn the line in public. Ajay Kumar Choudhary, its non-executive chairman and independent director, told the same event that “Decision making and execution must remain separate”, with AI free to recommend while authentication and final settlement follow deterministic auditable rules, MediaNama reported on 10 September 2026 [3].

Liability is what is holding it up. UPI’s whole dispute-resolution machinery was built around a human tapping approve on every transaction, and India Fintech Diaries quoted an industry source putting the gap as two questions, “how do you control a machine going rogue, and how does everyone involved get the information they need when something goes wrong” [1]. The delegation ceilings UPI already runs show how small the sanctioned blast radius is as things stand. UPI Circle caps full delegation at Rs 15,000 a month, and UPI Reserve Pay blocks up to Rs 10,000 for as long as 90 days [2].

The products shipped without the standard

Nobody on the show floor waited. Amazon Pay launched a Smart Wallet that lets AI agents make UPI payments for a user, with biometric authentication and offline tap-to-pay. Razorpay launched Vulcan, which it describes as India’s first transformer-based AI foundation model for payments, reading 3,000 signals per transaction for routing, fraud detection and personalisation. Pine Labs put an agent that books flights inside user-defined spending limits into its PLANET app, and BharatPe shipped a merchant assistant built on Google Gemini Enterprise that reaches more than 60 internal systems. NPCI itself released AiNxt, an open-source agentic platform, and AtOM, which writes signed machine-readable audit trails for UPI onboarding. MediaNama listed all of them on 11 September 2026 [4].

The same boundary turns up in a product built a long way from Mumbai. Sokin connected its licensed payment infrastructure to ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity through a Model Context Protocol connector on 14 September 2026 [5] [6]. A finance team can pull live balances, FX quotes and payment status, and prepare beneficiaries, conversions and payments, across licences held in 36 countries and settlement to more than 170 destinations [5]. In testing it handled ten multi-currency invoices and treasury moves in under ten minutes [5]. Sokin still presents every instruction to the customer for confirmation, and its existing approval rules still run before settlement [5]. Pete Daunton, Sokin’s chief strategy officer, put the pitch plainly: “The ability to give an agent real work is what is going to save our customers a lot of time” [5].

Read that list again and every product on it keeps a person in the approval step. The protocol that would have removed the person is the one that went back to the regulator.

item.title: CLARITY Act fails its Senate cloture vote
item.description: The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act failed its Senate cloture vote on 15 September 2026, short of the 60 votes it needed.
item.content:encoded:
The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act failed its cloture vote in the United States Senate on 15 September 2026, short of the 60 votes it needed to move to debate [1] [2]. CoinDesk’s live coverage said the failure essentially ends market structure legislative work in the Senate for 2026 [1].

The final text, 635 pages of it, had gone out on 14 September [3] [4]. One provision was written for the institutions a payments operator loses sleep over. If community banks were losing deposits to payment stablecoins on a substantial scale, the Treasury Secretary would have to restrict stablecoin rewards, and that power lapsed 18 months after the bill became law [3] [4]. Neither summary of the text says what counts as substantial [3] [4].

The banks wanted more than a trigger. Eight banking trade groups, the Bank Policy Institute among them, pushed for tighter limits on stablecoin rewards on 14 September [5] [6]. Their verdict on the circuit breaker, as AMBCrypto reported it on 15 September, was that one “that activates only after substantial deposit flight has already occurred is not a safeguard at all” [5].

The trigger goes down with the bill. What stays on the table is Treasury’s proposed rule under the GENIUS Act, on who needs a licence to issue a payment stablecoin and when a digital asset service provider may offer one to people in the United States, open for comment for 60 days from its Federal Register notice [7] [8].

Coinbase is wiring the small banks the vote was about

On 10 September Coinbase and Moov said Moov would build Coinbase Developer Platform custodial wallet accounts and its Payments API into the payments platform it runs for more than 1,000 community banks and credit unions in the United States [10] [11]. The uses listed are consumer stablecoin payments, merchant acceptance, settlement, payouts and real-time funding, run on the rails the institutions already use instead of a separate crypto stack [9] [10]. Wade Arnold, Moov’s chief executive, gave the reason: “Business customers of community institutions are already asked to accept stablecoins, and today they go outside their institution” [10].

The Senate fight was over whether stablecoin rewards drain deposits from small banks. This deal comes at it from the other end, by letting the business Arnold describes take the payment at its own credit union. Neither report gives a launch date or names the first institutions to go live [9] [10]. If your bank runs on Moov, ask for that list first, then ask where the stablecoins sit, because the product is built on Coinbase custodial accounts [9] [10].

The next date on the calendar is 18 January 2027, when the GENIUS Act takes effect [7] [8].

item.title: Worldline launches a UCP payment handler for AI orders
item.description: Worldline launched a Universal Commerce Protocol payment handler on 14 September 2026. Global Collect merchants can accept AI-initiated purchases.
item.content:encoded:
A quiet Monday. Worldline’s launch is today’s news. Paysera’s token reached Finextra on Friday 11 September [5], and the trade press picked it up again this morning [4].

Worldline launched a payment handler for the Universal Commerce Protocol on 14 September 2026 [1] [2]. UCP is the open standard for agentic commerce that Google co-developed with industry partners, and Worldline calls itself “one of the first in Europe” to plug into it [1]. A merchant declares its payment configuration once, then accepts cards, mobile wallets and European payment methods “across any UCP-connected AI platform” [1] [2]. The handler is available through Global Collect, Worldline’s cross-border payment platform [1].

The release has one market number, and it is borrowed: agent transactions could reach $3 trillion to $5 trillion by 2030, footnoted to a McKinsey report from October 2025 [1]. It does not name a single AI platform already live on the handler, and it says nothing about price or about who carries a dispute on an agent-initiated purchase [1].

If you already push cross-border volume through Global Collect, ask Worldline for the list of live UCP platforms and the chargeback terms before you build a checkout of your own.

Paysera gives an AI assistant a token that can draft a payment and stop there

Paysera, the Lithuanian electronic money institution, now lets clients create a personal access token and hand it to an AI assistant, an accounting program or an in-house system, free and with no separate agreement [3] [4]. The assistant reads an invoice, fills in the payee, the amount and the purpose, and leaves the transfer as a draft in the account [3]. “There is no automatic signing at this stage,” Paysera says; the client confirms every transfer with two-factor authentication [3]. The client decides which accounts the token can see, what it may do, its limits and how long it stays valid, and can switch it off at any time [3]. Paysera has also published a Paysera Payments skill, free and open source, for assistants such as Claude or Codex [3].

The reason given is PSD2. In the EU, payment initiation goes through licensed providers holding a certificate, “so an individual or a small business generally cannot get this kind of access to their own account”, the company says [3] [4]. Its chief executive, Justina Šidlauskienė, describes the design as “the software prepares, the human confirms” [3]. Paysera says it plans to add the exceptions strong customer authentication already allows, for trusted payees or business clients [3].

A scoped token with a human thumb on the button is a pattern a finance team can sign off this quarter. Watch the exceptions list. Once a trusted payee can skip the second factor, the token stops being a drafting tool and becomes a spending limit, and the client sets that limit. Paysera’s announcement puts no ceiling on it.

Sources

  1. Worldline press release on its Universal Commerce Protocol payment handler, 14 September 2026, read 14 September 2026
  2. FX News Group on the Worldline UCP payment handler, Maria Nikolova, 14 September 2026, read 14 September 2026
  3. Paysera blog, "the software prepares, the client confirms", read 14 September 2026
  4. Banking 4.0 on Paysera’s AI access tokens, 14 September 2026, read 14 September 2026

item.title: Ant International's agent protocol is live in ten wallets
item.description: Ant International's Agentic Mobile Protocol for AI agent payments is live in ten Alipay+ wallets through seven acquirers, including Adyen and Fiserv.
item.content:encoded:
It was a quiet weekend. Most of what follows was announced on Thursday 10 September and reached the trade press on Friday; Revolut’s disclosure, reported on Saturday, is the one new item.

Ant International’s Agentic Mobile Protocol, the open payment protocol it launched in April for AI agents paying through digital wallets, is now live in ten of them: Alipay, AlipayHK, DANA, GCash, KakaoPay, MPay, TNG eWallet, TrueMoney, Toss and Starryblu[1][2]. On the merchant side, seven acquirers carry it: Adyen, Allinpay, Checkout.com, Fiserv, Global Payments, Nuvei and Worldline[1][2]. The release, dated 10 September 2026, also puts the protocol on GitHub as open source, with SDKs and documentation[1][2].

The release makes two numeric claims. It says the protocol “cuts steps required to link a payment agent to a wallet by 50%”, and that its agent-to-agent settlement handles transactions “as tiny as $0.000001”[1]. Merchants get AgentSafePay, which it describes as a “money-back guarantee for merchants against agentic-specific risks”[1]. It does not say who funds that guarantee, how much it pays out, or which disputes count as agentic[1].

If you already take Alipay+ through one of those seven acquirers, agent-initiated wallet payments can reach you on the contract you already have, with no card-network pilot to sign. Put the three AgentSafePay blanks to the acquirer before a finance team counts on the guarantee.

Revolut sent KYC files in answer to a fake government request

Revolut confirmed that it disclosed sensitive customer information to an unauthorised third party after receiving fraudulent requests “sent from a legitimate government agency email domain”, TechCrunch reported on 12 September 2026[3]. According to the customer notice TechCrunch reviewed, the data included copies of passports and driving licences, and possibly verification selfies, account statements and transaction histories[3]. The Block’s list adds IBANs, withdrawal records and Bitcoin transaction histories[4]. Revolut declined to say how many customers were affected, whether one market was involved, or which agency’s domain was used[3][4]. Its spokesperson said “Revolut systems and customer funds are unaffected”[3].

A request from law enforcement lands in the one inbox a compliance team is trained to answer quickly. A real government domain proves that someone got into a government mailbox, so a callback to a number already on file is worth the day it costs before a passport scan leaves the building.

Nu pays 3.50% on USDC, and the Senate votes on stablecoin yield on 15 September

Nu opened in the United States on 10 September 2026. Its new Nu Global account converts deposits into USDC or EURC, “earning a daily yield of 3.50% APY and 2.20% APY, respectively”[5]. Nu Global moves money across more than 35 countries, and its integration with the US is “planned for the months ahead”, so for now it is not a US product[5]. Nu received conditional approval for a US national bank charter in January 2026[5].

The Senate’s cloture vote on the CLARITY Act is scheduled for Tuesday 15 September and needs 60 senators[6]. On 10 September nearly 80 state bankers associations joined the American Bankers Association and the Independent Community Bankers of America to press lawmakers to close what they call “the payment-of-interest loophole for payment stablecoins”[7]. Their letter warns that without amendments to Section 10404, the ambiguity could cause “a flight of deposits to stablecoins with real-world consequences”[6].

The vote is on Tuesday 15 September. Nu Global’s US integration is still “planned for the months ahead”, which puts it on the far side of whatever the Senate does about yield.

Sources

item.title: India's MyUPI adds real-time chargebacks
item.description: Reserve Bank of India Governor Sanjay Malhotra unveiled MyUPI on 10 September 2026. It adds automated real-time chargebacks for eligible UPI transactions.
item.content:encoded:
RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra unveiled MyUPI and UPI Tap & Pay at the Global Fintech Fest in Mumbai on 10 September 2026[1][2]. MyUPI puts a user’s UPI transactions and AutoPay mandates from every bank and app in one view, and it adds automated chargeback processing that “enables real-time chargeback creation for eligible transactions, significantly reducing complaint resolution time”[1]. Business Today describes the same feature as real-time chargebacks for eligible failed or disputed transactions, and says MyUPI runs on FiMI, NPCI’s in-house small language model[2].

It also carries a Safety Switch, which lets a user ask for UPI debits on their account to be declined when they suspect it has been compromised, plus a way to unlink a mobile number from receiving payments[1]. Before a payment goes out, it shows context about the payee[1]. Neither report gives a date for when MyUPI reaches phones[1][2].

Reuters reported on 10 September that NPCI plans a registry for AI agents paying on UPI, and the report says liability for wrong or unauthorised payments will need to be addressed through regulation[3]. Whoever ends up carrying that liability, the money comes back through a chargeback. A chargeback raised in real time is the piece of plumbing a payment made by software will lean on hardest, because an agent that pays the wrong merchant at 2am cannot be told to ring the bank on Monday.

Tap & Pay drops the PIN up to Rs 5,000

UPI Tap & Pay pays by tapping an NFC-enabled phone on a compatible point-of-sale terminal, with no PIN up to Rs 5,000 and a PIN above it[1][2]. It needs no mobile data or Wi-Fi, because the payment rides on the terminal’s connection[1][2]. Business Today reports that it uses tokens rather than exposing the payer’s bank details or UPI ID[2].

Tether and Fasanara want up to $3 billion for small-business credit

Tether and Fasanara Capital launched StableFund on 9 September 2026, a private credit fund with $400 million of committed co-investment and a target of up to $3 billion from third-party institutions[4][5]. Fasanara, a London asset manager with more than $6 billion under management, runs it[4][5]. Tether co-sponsors the fund, originates loans and supplies what the release calls “settlement infrastructure, including on/off-ramp connectivity and treasury rail integration”[4]. The money goes into short-duration, asset-backed loans to small businesses and consumers through fintech platforms in more than 60 countries[4][5].

The release says the structure embeds USDT into small-business and consumer lending flows, and it does not say whether a borrower receives the loan in USDT or pays it back in USDT[4].

Sources

item.title: Visa, Mastercard, Ant International to align agent checks
item.description: Visa, Mastercard and Ant International said on 9 September 2026 they will work towards common Know-Your-Agent principles for AI agents that pay.
item.content:encoded:
Visa, Mastercard and Ant International said on 9 September 2026 that they will work towards common principles for Know-Your-Agent, the checks a payment network runs to find out which business stands behind an AI agent before it lets the agent pay [1][2]. Each already runs a protocol of its own: Visa’s Trusted Agent Protocol, Mastercard Verifiable Intent and Ant International’s Agentic Mobile Protocol [1][2]. The work will go through BuildFin.ai, an industry platform convened by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, and builds on a framework called Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime [1].

The release sets out three pillars: tracing every agent to a validated operator, certifying agents against shared security and behaviour requirements, and monitoring them continuously on identity and transaction signals [1]. Its verb is a careful one. The three will “explore opportunities to work towards common principles” [1], and TNGlobal notes the participants gave no implementation timetable, pilot volumes or list of the merchants and banks that will test it [3]. The release cites McKinsey research projecting that AI agents will orchestrate US$3 trillion to 5 trillion of global consumer commerce by 2030 [1][2].

Of those pillars, monitoring is the one somebody has to staff. Tracing an agent to a company happens once, at onboarding, and certification is a test the agent passes on a particular day. Watching it afterwards is daily work, and it is the only pillar that catches an agent which was fine when it was certified and starts doing something odd four months later. The release does not say who pays for that.

India wants a register run by the rail

Reuters reported on 10 September, citing three sources involved in the discussions, that the National Payments Corporation of India plans a registry to verify and monitor AI agents that make payments on the Unified Payments Interface [4]. It sits inside NPCI’s planned Unified Agentic Protocol, would vet UPI agents first, and could later cover cards, bill payments and other payment methods [4]. One source said liability for wrong or unauthorised payments will need to be addressed through regulation [4]. ET Small Business, carried by RetailIntel, reports that the first transactions may be lower-value grocery transactions [5]. NPCI did not immediately respond to Reuters [4]. Yesterday’s brief carried the protocol as the Unified Agent Protocol; Reuters calls it the Unified Agentic Protocol.

That makes two models for the same check within a day. The card networks and Ant International are writing shared rules for the agents that touch their own networks, and India’s payments operator is building one register for everyone on its rail. Either way, an agent with no verified operator behind it does not get to pay.

Meta’s agent pays with a card built for one purchase

Meta launched Muse on 8 September, a personal agent that can open a browser, fill out forms and negotiate on the user’s behalf, and which asks before it sends an email or makes a purchase [6]. Checkout runs on Link, Stripe’s consumer network, which Stripe puts at more than 300 million users and more than 1 million businesses [7]. For every purchase the user approves the total in the chat, and Muse never sees the underlying payment details; at a retailer outside Link, Stripe issues Muse a single-use virtual card scoped to the approved purchase [7]. Meta says Muse is the first AI agent covered by Link’s purchase protections [6]. It is rolling out in the United States on iOS, Android and muse.ai [6], and TechCrunch lists a free tier alongside a Power plan at $20 a month and a Maximum plan at $100 [8].

A card that works only for the purchase the person approved is the cleanest answer to the mandate problem I have seen in a consumer product. It turns the dispute from “did I authorise this?” into “is this what I approved?”, and a support desk can settle the second question in a minute, provided somebody kept the approval screen.

Visa’s survey puts trust in AI payments at 23 per cent

Visa’s own research, published on 9 September, found that 72 per cent of US consumers have used an AI assistant [9], and only 23 per cent trust generative AI to handle payment transactions on their behalf [9][10]. Asked about Visa by name, 61 per cent said they would trust it to handle agentic transactions [9]. The Harris Poll ran the survey for Visa from 26 to 28 May 2026 across 2,065 US consumers, and between 1,028 and 1,034 of them answered the payment question for each brand tested [9][10]. It is Visa’s poll, and Visa is one of the brands it asked about.

The fix Visa put its name to that same day, with Mastercard and Ant International, starts a step before trust. Before an agent pays, the network finds out whose it is.

Sources

item.title: India's NPCI builds an AI agent protocol for UPI
item.description: Reuters reports the National Payments Corporation of India built a Unified Agent Protocol letting AI agents pay on UPI without per-transaction approval.
item.content:encoded:
The National Payments Corporation of India has built a framework called the Unified Agent Protocol, letting an AI agent execute payments on the Unified Payments Interface without a person approving each one. Reuters broke the framework at the start of September on three sources familiar with the plans, carried by Inc42 on 1 September and by Forkast today [1][2]. The two accounts do not sit flush. Forkast, writing today, says NPCI has not formally confirmed the protocol [1]. Inc42 lists it among what NPCI put in front of the Global Fintech Fest in Mumbai today, alongside AtOM, an agentic orchestration layer for integration and partner onboarding across UPI, and AiNxt, an in-house platform for building and deploying agents [3]. The fest runs to 11 September [3].

Nothing here is a new rail. UPI Circle already lets a primary account holder delegate payment authority to a secondary user, and the protocol seats an agent in that slot instead of a family member [1]. Reserve Pay already lets a customer block funds for multiple debits, capped at about Rs 10,000, roughly $105, for up to 90 days [1]. Forkast reports the transaction limits may follow NPCI’s existing rules for delegated payments from connected devices, Rs 15,000 a month and Rs 5,000 a transaction, with identity checks and audit trails on top [1]. The first use cases are groceries, subscriptions and cab bookings [1].

Both of those primitives already exist to answer the question of somebody who is not you spending your money, so reusing them is the cheapest way to ship this and it moves the hard engineering out of the payment entirely. Taking the money is solved. The part nobody has solved is the mandate: who set the limit, on what day, under which version of the app’s consent screen, and whether you can produce that record two months later when the customer says they never authorised a grocery order. Those are ledger questions, and the answer lives in whatever the logs actually captured at the time.

Mastercard shipped the merchant end the same day

Mastercard announced Agent Connect today, a single integration point through which merchants, AI agents, digital platforms and payment providers connect and transact [4][5]. It sits beside an expanded Mastercard Agent Suite for Merchants, which prepares product information for AI discovery and connects merchants to participating third-party agents [4]. Mastercard Agent Pay carries the transaction itself, on what CryptoBriefing describes as verifiable intents and tokenised, explicit consumer authorisation [5]. The launch is in the United States, with Samsung, Trip.com and Bemobi named [5]. Jorn Lambert, Mastercard’s chief product officer, said AI agents “are set to redefine the purchasing interface” and that the tools let businesses “maintain control over their destiny” [5].

PYMNTS Intelligence research carried with the announcement puts 46 per cent of merchants naming price, the final figure a customer pays, as the function they are least willing to surrender to an agent [4]. Thirty-one per cent plan to invest within a year in automated product search and comparison, and 26 per cent in letting an agent complete checkout on a shopper’s behalf [4]. Merchants will let an agent find the product, and rather fewer will let it close the sale. Price is where the willingness stops, and 46 per cent name it as the last thing they would hand over.

A flight is the first thing the PLANET app’s agent gets to buy

L&T Finance and Pine Labs announced at the same Mumbai fest that they are putting Pine Labs’ Agentic Storefront inside the L&T Finance PLANET app, with flight ticket bookings as the debut use case [6][7]. The shape is two agents. A buyer agent takes the customer’s stated intent inside guardrails set in the app, then discovers and pays for the flight. A seller agent connects to the airline’s own systems for live availability, fares and booking data, so the options coming back are ones that can actually be fulfilled [6]. Payment runs over P3P, Pine Labs’ own protocol for autonomous UPI payments, with a layer called Grantex holding authorisation delegation, identity verification, spend controls and auditability [6]. L&T Finance puts its customer database above 2.9 crore, about 29 million [6]. Manish Kumar Gupta, chief executive for urban unsecured assets, payments and digital partnerships at L&T Finance, called it “a major shift from conversational assistance to true transaction execution” [6].

The seller agent is the unglamorous half and it decides whether any of this holds up. An agent that returns a fare which has gone by the time the payment lands produces a refund and a support ticket instead of a flight, and produces both faster than a person would have. Starting on airline seats is a choice worth respecting, and it is no soft opening. Airline inventory moves by the second, so the integration has to be honest in real time or the whole flow reads as broken to the customer.

All three leave the same thing open. An agent buys the wrong item on a Tuesday night, and somebody has to pay for it. Forkast reports the Indian framework leans on liability following control, spreading responsibility across banks, payment providers, merchants and AI providers so a consumer does not have to work out whose algorithm failed before getting their money back [1]. Liability following control is a principle rather than a rule, and nobody has published the version a customer service agent could read off a screen at eleven at night. Reserve Pay’s cap is Rs 10,000.

Sources

item.title: Circle buys Tazapay for $400 million in stock
item.description: Circle agreed on 8 September 2026 to buy the Singapore cross-border payments company Tazapay for $400 million in stock. It is expected to close in 2027.
item.content:encoded:
Circle announced today that it has agreed to buy Tazapay, a Singapore cross-border payments company, for $400 million in Circle Class A common stock [1]. The deal is expected to close in 2027 and needs approval from the Monetary Authority of Singapore alongside the usual closing conditions [1]. Tazapay runs about $25 billion in annualised payment volume, works with more than 60 banking and fintech partners, and holds local payout rails in more than 100 markets; Circle puts stablecoins at more than 60 per cent of that volume as of 31 July 2026 [2]. Irfan Ganchi, senior vice president of payments at Circle, said the acquisition “will increase Circle’s capability to originate and terminate payments globally, near-instant and 24/7” [1].

Originate and terminate is the operator’s half of that sentence. A stablecoin has always moved value between two wallets in seconds. The expensive part is the last mile, getting money into a local bank account in a market where you hold no licence and no bank relationship. Circle has spent two years selling the middle. Today it paid $400 million for a hundred markets of the ends.

Anthropic is advertising for the people who would replace Stripe

The Information reported this month that Anthropic is working out which parts of billing, payments, fraud detection and tax it should build itself rather than buy, and pointed at the company’s own job adverts as the evidence [3]. The Billing Platform team is hiring a staff software engineer whose scope runs to pricing primitives, payments infrastructure, contracts, entitlements, revenue pipelines and reconciliation [3]. Revenue last quarter was $11.5 billion, against $787 million a year earlier [3]. An Anthropic spokesperson told The Information that “Stripe has been a strong partner to Anthropic for years, and we continue to work with them” [3]. The Information sits behind a paywall and was not read in full here. CryptoBriefing carried the report on 4 September, saying only that Stripe handles a substantial part of Anthropic’s financial plumbing and giving no figures [4]; PYMNTS wrote it up today with the numbers attached [3].

Taking a card payment is a solved problem, and Stripe solved it. Metering a token-priced product across contracts, credits, committed spend and enterprise entitlements, then tying a month of usage events back to an invoice a finance team will sign, is a ledger problem wearing a payments costume. That is the part that keeps people in the office at month end, and it is the part the job advert describes. Adyen bought Orb for about $335 million in July [3]. Adyen paid $335 million rather than build that layer. Anthropic is advertising for it at staff-engineer rates.

Mastercard puts a number on 2030

Mastercard published A Short History of the Future of Shopping and Payments today, built on research run with Opinium in June and July across 26,000 parents and teenagers aged 13 to 18 in 13 countries, and on the readings of four futurists: Magnus Lindkvist, Patrick Dixon, Katja Forbes and Theodora Lau [5][6]. It expects more than one in ten online shoppers, upwards of 300 million people, to be routinely using AI agents to buy by 2030, and puts AI-driven consumer spending at about £370 billion a year by then [5]. Eighteen per cent of the teenagers surveyed already use an AI assistant weekly to compare prices [5]. The two outlets that carried the report print different figures for the parent comparison and for how many teenagers would hand a purchase over entirely, so those numbers stay out of this brief; Mastercard’s own newsroom page returned a 403 here, and so did Payment Expert’s write-up.

Lau’s contribution, as Financial IT read it, is a prediction that at least three G20 regulators will issue guidance on registering and monitoring AI agents by 2030 [6]. Four years is a comfortable runway for a rulebook and a tight one for a dispute process. When an agent buys the wrong thing at three in the morning under a delegated mandate, who eats it: the issuer, the merchant, or the company that shipped the model? None of the three has printed an answer.

Sources

item.title: KPMG: fintech investment hits $103.1 billion in H1 2026
item.description: KPMG's Pulse of Fintech counts $103.1 billion of global fintech investment in the first half of 2026 and names agentic commerce as a second-half theme.
item.content:encoded:
KPMG’s Pulse of Fintech for the first half of 2026 was back in the news on Monday, carried by ANI at 6:12pm Indian time under a headline about agentic commerce [1]. The report itself has been out since August [2]. Global fintech investment across venture, private equity and mergers rose from $72.2 billion in the second half of 2025 to $103.1 billion in the first half of 2026, on 2,100 deals against 2,500 the half before [2]. Ten deals made $64 billion of that, 62 per cent, led by Global Payments buying Worldpay for $24.3 billion and FIS buying Global Payments’ issuer solutions business for $13.5 billion [2]. The Americas took $86.9 billion and the United States $80.8 billion of it across 933 deals, while EMEA drew $11.3 billion and Asia-Pacific $4.6 billion [2].

The agentic line sits on the predictions page, second of five. KPMG expects the use of AI agents to shop and transact for people and companies to pull money into the work around it, and it names cybersecurity and digital identity management first, so that “such transactions are approved, safeguarded, and well-protected from bad actors,” with payments solutions and infrastructure built for agents after that [2]. The payments section adds the line I read twice: modernised rails will have to coexist with instant payment systems, and it names Pix and UPI, next to stablecoin and tokenisation infrastructure [2]. FintechNews Switzerland ran the same predictions on 2 September, with Natural’s $30 million Series A in July for agent payment infrastructure and Mastercard’s purchase of BVNK in August as its worked examples [3].

Approved is the word doing the work. A scheme that can say which agent, acting for whom, under what limit, is what an operations team asks for before it lets an agent near a settlement account, and it is the piece EMVCo only put out for comment on 1 September, with responses due by the end of the month (the 2 September edition). The money KPMG expects to flow into agent identity is going into that question, not past it.

Mumbai this week

The Global Fintech Fest opens in Mumbai on 8 September and runs to the 11th at the Jio World Centre and Trident BKC, organised by the Payments Council of India, NPCI and the Fintech Convergence Council, with agentic AI first in its theme line [4]. Reuters reported on 1 September, per Inc42, that NPCI is preparing a Unified Agent Protocol to let an AI agent make UPI payments without the user approving each one, built on the existing UPI Circle delegation and Reserve Pay features, and that NPCI has already shown a pilot [5]. No cap, limit or launch date has been printed anywhere I can find. If the protocol lands on a stage this week, KPMG’s sentence about UPI and agent infrastructure coexisting gets a worked example within a month of the report.

A quiet weekend

Nothing else in agentic commerce or AI payments cleared this desk’s two-source bar between Saturday and Monday morning. The items in circulation were re-reports of stories this brief already carried: the 21-bank dollar stablecoin from 1 September, Swift’s shared-ledger payment for Siemens from 4 September and the Pix to TIPS study from Saturday. On the rulebook, the Comptroller of the Currency, Jonathan Gould, has said he wants final GENIUS Act rules out by November so applications can be processed in the new year, per PYMNTS on 20 August [6].

Ten deals made $64 billion of KPMG’s $103.1 billion, and the biggest was a payments processor changing hands. Agentic commerce is on the prediction page.

Sources

item.title: Brazil's Pix and Europe's TIPS weigh a link, pilot in 2028
item.description: The European Central Bank and Banco Central do Brasil are assessing a link between TIPS and Pix. A pilot is pencilled in for June 2028.
item.content:encoded:
Reuters reported on 3 September 2026 that technical teams at the European Central Bank and Banco Central do Brasil are assessing whether Pix and TIPS can be connected, citing sources close to the work. The ECB told Reuters there is “an ongoing preliminary investigation exploring a potential interlinking” between its TARGET Instant Payment Settlement platform and Pix, and that it named Pix a currency corridor under exploration in June [1]. Brazil’s central bank declined to comment [1].

Folha de S.Paulo had the internal schedule the same day. An internal Banco Central document puts nine of the bank’s departments on the study, with the pre-investigation stage, legal, technical, operational and security, due to finish this month [2][3]. Deeper feasibility work runs from October 2026 to March 2027, an implementation phase from April 2027 to June 2028 waits on approval by both central banks, a technical corridor is pencilled in for November 2027 and an operational pilot for June 2028 [2][4]. A committee of the bank’s deputy heads visits the ECB in October [2].

TIPS is the Eurosystem’s settlement layer for instant euro payments, and the ECB has spent two years wiring it to other countries’ rails. Exploratory work with India’s Unified Payments Interface opened in October 2024, the Governing Council moved that link to a realisation phase on 20 November 2025, a feasibility assessment with Switzerland’s SIC Instant Payments system opened in September 2025, and a connection to Nexus Global Payments, which joins the fast payment systems of Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and India, is still under exploration [5][6]. Pix would be the first of the named corridors outside Europe and Asia [5].

Seven months separate the technical corridor in November 2027 from the June 2028 pilot. That is where the settlement mechanics and the legal agreements get argued over, and the schedule already says the implementation phase cannot start until both central banks approve it. The UPI link took thirteen months to get from exploratory phase to realisation phase [5].

Thailand approves stablecoin principles and publishes nothing

Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission approved a set of principles on 3 September 2026 to tighten oversight of stablecoin transactions by digital asset businesses, per a report at coindesk.cc that cites the regulator’s own channels and gives no requirement, threshold or effective date [7]. The Bangkok Post’s report on the same decision sits behind a paywall and the SEC’s release was not reachable this morning, so what the principles ask of an exchange or a custodian is not printed here.

A quiet weekend

Nothing else in agentic commerce or AI payments cleared the desk’s two-source bar in the last 48 hours. The items doing the rounds on Friday were re-reports of stories this brief already carried: Anthropic’s commerce agent blueprint from 2 September, the Siemens payment on Swift’s shared ledger from the 4 September edition, and Singapore’s stablecoin consultation from 1 September. The Global Fintech Fest in Mumbai, where NPCI is expected to show agent payments on UPI, opens this week.

Brazil’s central bank has nine departments on the Pix link and no comment on it.

item.title: Stablecoin supply stalls after a two-year climb
item.description: Bloomberg reported on 4 September 2026 that stablecoin growth has stalled after a two-year climb. Circle puts USDC at $73.3 billion at the end of June.
item.content:encoded:
Stablecoin supply has stopped growing. Bloomberg reported on 4 September 2026 that growth has stalled after a two-year climb, with weaker crypto trading cutting demand for the tokens traders use to park cash, and that the pause lands just as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been selling stablecoin issuers as a new source of demand for Treasury bills [1].

Circle’s own quarterly releases carry the same story in two numbers. USDC in circulation was $77.0 billion at the end of March 2026 and $73.3 billion at the end of June [2][3]. This morning DefiLlama reads USDC at $74.7 billion and Tether’s USDT at $183.4 billion, and CoinGecko reads $74.6 billion and $183.4 billion, so the two aggregators agree on the two coins that carry most of the market [4][5]. They disagree on the total, DefiLlama counting $311 billion of dollar-pegged supply against $291 billion in CoinGecko’s stablecoin category, because each counts a different set of tokens [4][5]. PYMNTS, citing CoinDesk and RWA.xyz, put the fall from the May peak at about $10 billion by mid-July, roughly 3 per cent and the biggest such decline since 2023 [6].

At Jackson Hole on 27 August, Pablo Hernández de Cos of the Bank for International Settlements said tokenised deposits keep the tight link to deposit-taking that stablecoins do not, and that the same stablecoin on two different chains is not interoperable without risky or costly workarounds, per Payments Dive [7].

If you settle in stablecoins, the supply chart is the least of it. The working question is which chain your counterparty’s USDC sits on, and the BIS has now said so at a Federal Reserve symposium.

Williams-Sonoma’s assistant converts at three times the rate

Sameer Hassan, chief technology and digital officer at Williams-Sonoma, told the company’s second quarter earnings call on 26 August 2026 that customers who use Olive, the assistant on the Williams Sonoma site, convert at three times the rate of those who do not [8][9]. Engagement with Olive is up 700 per cent since the start of the year and revenue attributed to it is up 620 per cent [8][10]. Otto, the Pottery Barn assistant that rolled out in August, resolves over 70 per cent of engagements without handing the customer to a person [9][10]. A personalised visit now generates roughly nine times the revenue of an average visit, against two times a year ago [9][10].

The percentages start from a base the company does not print. Olive lives on the merchant’s site, the merchant keeps the checkout, and the model never holds a card. That is the version of agentic commerce producing numbers on an earnings call.

Stripe hires for stablecoin cards

Stripe has hired Drew Turchin to lead its stablecoin-based card business, Payments Dive reported on 3 September [11]. He arrives from Native Markets, the startup that issued the USDH stablecoin with Hyperliquid, and before that ran business development, partnerships and ventures at Uniswap Labs in New York [11]. Coingape had the appointment on 27 August, placing him with Henri Stern and Max Segall on Stripe’s stablecoin card team [12]. In the LinkedIn post announcing the role, Turchin wrote that cards are “making those balances instantly spendable in everyday life” [11].

PicPay lets Claude read the ledger and not touch it

PicPay, the Brazilian payments app, announced on 3 September 2026 that customers can ask Claude about their accounts after authenticating in PicPay: balances, outstanding bills, investments, active cards, favourite Pix contacts, recent transactions and card statements [13]. It is free on Android and iOS, rolls out through an early-access list, works on any Claude tier, and follows a ChatGPT plugin the company shipped earlier [13][14]. The experience does not support financial transactions through Claude [14]. The model reads the ledger, and nothing it says moves money.

The Global Fintech Fest opens at the Jio World Centre in Mumbai on 8 September and runs to 11 September [15]. Reuters, via Deccan Chronicle, reports that NPCI plans to use it to unveil the Unified Agent Protocol, which would let an AI agent pay on UPI inside limits the user sets in advance, built on UPI Circle and Reserve Pay [16][17].

item.title: Swift's blockchain ledger moves Siemens' treasury money
item.description: Swift's blockchain-based shared ledger carried its first corporate treasury payment this week, for Siemens, from BNP Paribas in euros to HSBC in sterling.
item.content:encoded:
Swift’s blockchain-based shared ledger carried a corporate treasury payment this week, the first one it has handled [1][2]. The money belonged to Siemens. It left a euro account at BNP Paribas in France and arrived in sterling at HSBC in the United Kingdom [1][2].

The pilot was testing whether a shared ledger can reach across two separate banking systems while the value stays in commercial bank money [2].

Citi is live, and the phase closes in December

Citi processed live transactions on the same ledger on 2 September 2026, the first US bank to do so, working with First Abu Dhabi Bank in the Middle East and Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation in Southeast Asia [3][4]. DBS and United Overseas Bank are due later this month [3]. The controlled proof-of-concept phase runs from July to December 2026 [3].

Citi published two of its own numbers alongside the announcement. Its 24/7 US dollar clearing serves more than 300 bank clients, and Citi Token Services processes about $1 billion in transactions, a figure the release prints with no period attached [3]. Neither figure went over Swift’s ledger. They describe the size of the business the ledger would have to be good enough to carry.

A phase with a stated end forces a decision in January. Either the ledger goes into production or it joins the shelf of well-documented pilots.

Australia said no to a digital dollar and opened RITS instead

The Reserve Bank of Australia and the Treasury concluded again that there is no clear public interest case for a retail central bank digital currency, holding the position they set in the 2024 white paper [5][6]. Crypto News Australia reports the finding rests on consumer research by Verian Group, which found Australians well served by the payment methods they already have [6].

Alongside that finding, the bank opened a consultation on the role of RITS, its real-time settlement system, and the Fast Settlement Service in a tokenised financial system. The RBA is seeking feedback by 30 October 2026 [7]. It asks four things: how tokenised asset platforms could synchronise with RITS and the FSS for delivery-versus-payment settlement in central bank reserves, how those systems could exchange different institutions’ tokenised private money one for one and against ordinary bank accounts, what account structures and access models would let stablecoin issuers hold central bank reserves, and how tokenised reserves would be issued, distributed and funded [7].

So the RBA will not issue a token to consumers, and is asking the market how it should settle the tokens that banks and stablecoin issuers issue instead.

TabaPay is buying its own bank charter

TabaPay closed $155 million of strategic growth financing on 2 September 2026, led by FTV Capital, and said it intends to acquire Transact Bank, a Denver bank with an Office of the Comptroller of the Currency charter [8][9]. Transact becomes TabaBank. The acquisition is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to regulatory approval [8].

Every payments company that scales runs into the same wall. The sponsor bank sets the risk appetite, the settlement windows and the price, and it can revisit all three on its own timetable. Buying a charter costs money and time, and it turns a technology company into an institution with examiners in the building.

Rodney Robinson, TabaPay’s chief executive, says TabaBank will bring payments and banking under one roof while the company keeps working alongside its network of bank partners [8]. If regulators approve, TabaPay will also be one of them.

Sources

item.title: Anthropic publishes commerce agent blueprints for Claude
item.description: Anthropic published commerce agent blueprints on 2 September 2026: working shopping and merchant agents for retail, travel, telecom and ticketing.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic published blueprints yesterday for building shopping and merchant agents on Claude, aimed at retailers going into the holiday season [1][2]. Not a product. Working reference implementations, across retail, travel, telecom and ticketing, shipped as something an engineering team clones [2].

The shopping agent searches a product catalogue, assembles multi-item carts, tailors recommendations to a customer, shows comparisons inside the conversation, hands the finished cart to checkout, and answers questions about orders, returns, exchanges and refund policy [2]. The merchant agent answers questions about sales performance, watches inventory, flags problems, recommends pricing and promotions off sales history, and drafts marketing campaigns [2]. Either one deploys through the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry or Google Cloud Vertex AI, and there is a Claude Code plugin [2].
